The authors concluded that in this protocol, trans-oral neuro-stimulation did not result in changes in genioglossal activity or upper airway collapse; however, other beneficial effects were observed suggesting a need for additional mechanistic investigation. These researchers stated that further investigation is needed across a broader cohort r to examine the ideal patient population for this device.

The authors stated that this study had several drawbacks. First, given the invasive nature of the physiological assessments, the sample size was modest; therefore, this trial was clearly under-powered for small effect sizes or subgroup analyses. Although these researchers did not see systematic differences in genioglossus activity between groups, they acknowledged that these recordings were highly variable; thus, they may require a large sample to see statistical significance or to identify which subsets respond best to therapy. Future investigations should be directed towards clinical outcomes rather than surrogate metrics. In addition, some individuals who passed screening had higher AHIs than intended based on inclusion criteria on PSG; thus, this cohort was likely more heterogenous than intended. Second, the rigorous measurement of snoring is notoriously difficulty since self‐report, bed partner report, objective measurements etc. all give slightly different information. These investigators used both snoring as well as objective quantification of inspiratory flow limitation to attempt to examine any effect but arguably none was definitive; therefore, they encouraged further efforts in this context. Third, despite the authors’ best efforts, treatment adherence was not 100%, which may have decreased the impact of the intervention. These researchers considered this finding as the nature of human research rather than a major deficiency in their approach or in the technology they were evaluating. Notably, these investigators viewed it as a limitation that this model of the device did not allow for correlation of device intensity and clinical outcomes. Newer versions of the device have cloud‐based monitoring with adherence and intensity data routinely available. Fourth, this trial did not have a sham control group; thus, these investigators could not rule out changes based on time or repeat testing. The authors noted that despite these drawbacks, they viewed these findings as important and hoped that they would lead to further investigations in this area.

Moffa et al (2023) stated that recently, new non-invasive ES devices have been developed with the objective to increase the tongue muscle tone for patients with OSA and snorers. In a systematic review, these investigators examined the first results found in the literature regarding the effectiveness of non-invasive ES devices for the treatment of primary snoring and OSA. These researchers carried out an electronic search on PubMed/Medline, Google Scholar, and Ovid databases; the PRISMA statement was followed. Databases were searched from inception through September, 2021. A total of 4 studies met the criteria for inclusion in this review, for a total of 265 patients. Two devices were included in this review, Apone-Stim 400 Muscle Stimulator and eXciteOSA. All studies suggested that these new devices were effective in improving snoring by approximately 50% after device training, without major complications; however data regarding OSA improvement were conflicting. The authors concluded that intra-oral non-invasive ES devices could be considered a valid option to current therapies for snoring. Moreover, these researchers stated that further studies are needed to support these interesting new devices for treatment of OSA.

Nokes et al (2023) noted that OSA is a common disorder with major neurocognitive and cardiovascular sequelae. The treatment of symptomatic patients with mild OSA remains controversial given that adherence to positive airway pressure (PAP) has historically been sub-optimal. In an open-label study, these researchers examined a daily trans-oral NMES device for individuals with mild OSA. The sample represents a subset of participants with a baseline AHI of 5 to 14.9 events/hour, drawn from a parent study that also included subjects with primary snoring. Outcome measures for the current study included changes in AHI, ESS, PSQI and snoring levels before and after use of the NMES. Among 65 participants (68% men) with median age of 49 years (range of 24 to 79) and median BMI of 27.7 kg/m2 (range of 20 to 34), the NMES device was used daily for 6 weeks. We observed a significant improvement in the AHI from 10.2 to 6.8 events/hour among all participants and from 10.4 to 5.0 events/hour among responders. Statistically significant improvements in the ESS, PSQI, objectively measured snoring, and bed partner-reported snoring were observed. Adherence among all participants was 85%. The authors concluded that this NMES device had the benefit of being a treatment modality of daytime therapy that rendered a high level of tolerability and patient acceptance. It alleviated the need for an in-situ device during sleep and resulted in improvements in OSA severity, snoring, and subjective sleep metrics, potentially crucial in mild OSA. Moreover, these researchers stated that further investigations are needed to define which individuals may benefit most from the device across the wider spectrum of OSA severity and examine long-term therapeutic outcomes.

The authors stated that this study had several drawbacks. First, the absence of a sham comparator meant that the observed improvements may have been a result of a placebo effect and/or non-specific changes in health behavior such as diet, exercise, or alcohol intake. However, these investigators did not instruct the subjects on any of these factors; therefore, they doubted any major change in health behavior during this trial given the longstanding nature of the snoring complaints and short therapy period of 6 weeks. In addition, the possibility of a placebo effect was partially mitigated by the inclusion of objectively assessed endpoints, and the fact that consistent changes were observed for objectively measured and self-reported endpoints. However, ongoing clinical trials do include a control arm. Second, the open-label nature of the study prevented the sleep study staff from being blinded to the pre- or post-therapy status of the patient. More importantly, the sleep studies were analyzed using the validated auto-scoring algorithms in the zzzPAT software (Itamar Medical), with manual adjustment limited to reviewing the signals for irregularities/artifacts; thereby, minimizing the possibility that the lack of blinding impacted the interpretation of the objective snoring, AHI, or ODI endpoints. In addition, the primary statistical analysis was carried out by an independent statistician. Third, these researchers did not evaluate hard outcomes such as cardiovascular disease endpoints or neurocognitive performance. These outcomes remain the key endpoints to consider and should be assessed in larger long-term studies. Although the authors have shown a reduction in clinical indices associated with sleep-disordered breathing, they could not conclusively determine whether their interventions resulted in the desired improvements in OSA complications. Ongoing clinical trials include polysomnography in order to better examine the differences in rapid eye movement (REM) versus non-REM AHI as well as the impact of sleep position. Furthermore, it’s worth mentioning that these researchers excluded individuals with a BMI of greater than 35 kg/m2 as they believed it was less likely that NMES will have a treatment effect in morbid obesity. Fourth, these investigators did not study the mechanisms underlying their observed improvements; but have ongoing efforts to record genioglossus muscle function before and after stimulation to examine these mechanistic aspects. Additionally, these investigators believed that their therapeutic approach may be helpful for particular OSA endophenotypes (such as those with lower upper airway gain) which they plan to study in future investigations.

Abreu et al (2023) stated that mild OSA is a common disorder associated with daytime sleepiness and impaired QOL. Given that adherence to PAP therapy in OSA is suboptimal, alternative strategies are needed especially for patients with mild OSA. Daytime NMES of the tongue is a new therapeutic modality for mild OSA. In a randomised, sham-controlled, double-masked controlled study, these researchers examined if patients with mild OSA adhere to daytime NMES for the recommended period. This trial was carried out in 40 patients with mild OSA who received either high-intensity (active) or low-intensity (sham) NMES for 6 weeks. The primary end-point was adherence to therapy. Exploratory outcomes included the respiratory event index (REI) and the ESS score. More than 90% of subjects in each arm were adherent to NMES. Exploratory analyses showed a 32.7% (95% CI: 15.5% to 49.9%) drop in the REI with active NMES, with no significant change in the REI with sham NMES. Improvements were larger in the supine than non-supine REI. Both the apnea index and hypopnea index improved with active NMES. Finally, the ESS score improved with active but not with sham NMES. The authors concluded that daytime NMES was well-accepted, with a majority of participants using it for the recommended period; NMES of the tongue use was associated with improvements in OSA severity and daytime sleepiness. Moreover, these researchers stated that further investigations are needed to define its role in the treatment armamentarium across the spectrum of OSA severity and in patients who are intolerant to PAP therapy.

The authors stated that drawbacks of this trial included the small sample size (40 participants with mild OSA: 21 to the active arm and 19 to the sham arm), restriction to mild OSA and lack of follow-up beyond 6 weeks. A larger sample size with longer follow-up would aid in defining the heterogeneity of treatment effects and assessment of the resiliency. These issues notwithstanding, the findings of this study provided evidence on the adherence to active and sham NMES along with preliminary data on the effectiveness of a novel treatment approach for mild OSA. These investigators stated that further work across the spectrum of OSA severity is needed to anchor the use of daytime NMES in OSA.

Measurement of Serum/Plasma Brain-Derived Neurotrophic Factor (BDNF) Levels as a Biomarker for Diagnosis of OSA

Khalaji et al (2023) stated that chronic intermittent hypoxia associated with OSA could affect neurons and glial cells, resulting in cell stress and damage, and changes in brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF) levels. In a systematic review and meta-analysis, these investigators examined the relation between BDNF, OSA, and CPAP (the standard of care [SOC] in patients with OSA). A total of 5 databases were searched for studies that examined serum and/or plasma BDNF levels in patients with OSA and controls or publications examining the effect of CPAP treatment on BDNF levels. These investigators used SMDs with its 95% CI comparison between patients with OSA and controls. A total of 10 studies were included in this meta-analysis examining the relation between BDNF levels, OSA, and CPAP treatment; 5 studies of BDNF levels in OSA compared to controls showed no significant difference (SMD = - 0.52, 95% CI: - 1.93 to 0.89, p-value = 0.47). No statistically significant difference was found between CPAP treatment in patients with OSA and BDNF levels (SMD = - 0.78, 95% CI: - 1.77 to 0.21, p-value = 0.12). The authors concluded that BDNF peripheral levels were not significantly altered in OSA or by its related treatment, preventing its use as a biomarker.

Measurement of Serum/Plasma Insulin-Like Growth Factor 1 (IGF-1) Levels for Diagnosis of Obstructive Sleep Apnea Hypopnea Syndrome (OSAHS)

He et al (2022) noted that OSAHS is a common disease that has serious cardiovascular and metabolic effects. Insulin-like growth factor 1 (IGF-1) levels are reportedly reduced in patients with OSAHS; however, this is still a matter of debate. In a meta-analysis, these investigators examined the association between serum/plasma IGF-1 levels and OSAHS. Wan Fang, Excerpta Medica dataBASE, Web of Science, China National Knowledge Infrastructure, VIP, PubMed, and other databases were searched for materials published in any language before April 2, 2022. Two researchers analyzed the studies for quality according to the Newcastle-Ottawa Scale. The acquired data were analyzed using Stata 11.0 and R 3.6.1 software. The effect size was estimated and calculated using SMDs and CIs. Moreover, a combined analysis was carried out using either a random- or fixed-effects model. A total of 34 studies met the inclusion criteria. These findings showed that the plasma/serum IGF-1 concentrations in patients with OSAHS was significantly reduced compared with those in healthy subjects. Subgroup analyses were carried out according to OSAHS severity, ethnicity, age, BMI, specimen testing method, and study design. The outcomes suggested that nearly all subgroups of patients with OSAHS had reduced serum IGF-1 levels. Disease severity and differences in ethnicity were identified as possible influencing factors of serum IGF-1 levels in patients with OSAHS in the meta-regression analysis, and no other factors were found to alter plasma/serum IGF-1 concentrations. Moreover, plasma/serum IGF-1 concentrations were negatively correlated with AHI and oxygen desaturation index scores and positively associated with minimum oxygen saturation. The authors concluded that serum/plasma IGF-1 concentrations in patients with OSAHS were greatly reduced compared with those of patients in the control group; and were negatively correlated with AHI and oxygen desaturation index scores and positively correlated with minimum oxygen saturation. Moreover, these researchers stated that further well-designed studies are needed to examine the association between IGF-1 concentration and OSAHS risk.

The authors stated that this study had several drawbacks. First, this study may have included confounding variables, such as age, smoking history, lifestyle, alcohol consumption, sex, and diabetes. In particular, diabetes may be a major confounding factor for circulating IGF-1 levels. Moreover, OSA is more common in men, the elderly, and individuals with obesity compared with the general population. These investigators were unable to control for the afore-mentioned confounding factors because the included studies did not provide data on past medical history, specific lifestyle factors, or analysis by sex, and no studies were carried out only in older patients with OSAHS. To a greater or lesser extent, several potential confounding factors might have influenced the final findings. Second, the EEG fragmentation index and N3 sleep (SWS) were identified as important indicators in the evaluation of OSAHS; however, the included studies did not examine the direct relationship between serum/plasma IGF-1 levels, EEG fragmentation index and SWS. Third, these researchers were unable to conclude a causal association between serum/plasma IGF-1 concentrations and OSAHS in this investigation because of the lack of an appropriate longitudinal cohort study. Fourth, most of the studies included were small sample studies comprised of less than 100 cases, which was insufficient to confirm an association between IGF-1 and OSAHS.

Measurement of Serum/Plasma Monocyte Chemoattractant Protein-1 (MCP-1) Levels for Diagnosis of OSA

Imani et al (2022) stated that among the broad variety of chemokines, monocyte chemoattractant protein-1 (MCP-1) is considered to be one of the most important chemokines. Among others, MCP-1 activates monocytes and other immune cells highly involved in inflammation. In a systematic review and meta-analysis, these investigators examined the relationship between serum/plasma MCP-1 levels and the risk of OSA in adults as a disease related to inflammation. A total of 4 databases were systematically examined until July 12, 2022. These researchers employed the Review Manager 5.3 software to extract and calculate the SMD and its 95% CI of plasma/serum levels of MCP-1 between adults with and without OSA. A total of 8 articles including 11 studies in adults were entered into the meta-analysis. The serum/plasma MCP-1 levels in adults with OSA were higher than that in the controls (SMD = 0.81; p = 0.0007) and as well as for adults with severe OSA compared to those with mild and moderate OSA (SMD = 0.42; p < 0.0001). The subgroup analysis showed that ethnicity was an effective factor in the pooled analysis of blood MCP-1 levels in adults with OSA compared to the controls (Asians: (p < 0.0001), mixed ethnicity: (p = 0.04), and Caucasians: (p = 0.89)). The meta-regression showed increasing serum/plasma MCP-1 levels in adults with OSA versus the controls, publication year, age of controls, BMI of controls, and sample size reduced, and also BMI and the AHI of adults with OSA increased. The authors concluded that the findings of this meta-analysis showed that serum/plasma levels of MCP-1 in adults with OSA were significantly higher than those in controls, as well as in adults with severe OSA compared to mild/moderate OSA; thus, it appeared that MCP-1 could have a practical, clinical, and diagnostic importance in adults with OSA. In addition, age, ethnicity, BMI, and AHI should be considered in the diagnostic and therapeutic approach to adults with OSA.

The authors stated that this study had several drawbacks. First, there was a low number of cases in most of the studies. Second, there was a high heterogeneity in the initial pooled analysis. Third, the occurrence of several confounding factors. Fourth, some of the studies reported the MCP-1 level on the graphs and these researchers estimated their means (and SDs) with appropriate software. Fifth, there was a publication bias between or across the studies.

NightLase Laser Therapy for the Treatment of Snoring or Obstructive Sleep Apnea

The Fotona NightLase therapy is a non-invasive laser therapy used on the oral mucosa tissue for reducing the effects and amplitude of snoring.

Shiffman et al (2021) stated that OSA is a serious condition; however, its treatment is often not effective or is poorly accepted by patients. Newer modes of therapy that are more effective and also more accepted by patients need to be developed. The latest therapeutic approaches entail a minimally invasive LAUP procedure. This procedure involves thermal processing of the relaxed soft palate and surrounding tissues using neodymium-doped yttrium aluminum garnet (Nd:YAG) and erbium-doped yttrium aluminum garnet (Er:YAG) lasers, resulting in favorable collagen shrinkage and development of new collagen fibers. Procedure has previously been reported to safely and effectively reduce snoring, as well as increase the volume of the oropharyngeal airway, and is well-accepted by patients. These researchers examined the effectiveness of minimally invasive outpatient LAUP procedure (NightLase LAUP) to reduce AHI in patients with OSA. The effectiveness of the minimally invasive LAUP procedure, combining Nd:YAG laser (λ = 1,064 nm) and Er:YAG laser (λ = 2,940 nm) applied to the soft palate for treatment of OSA on 27 patients with different severities of OSA was evaluated based on AHI measurements before and after only three 20-min sessions in an outpatient setting over a period of 45 to 60 days. A decrease in AHI for all the patients with different severities of OSA tested in this study was achieved, with 66.3% average improvement (32% to 100%); and 50% or more improvement was achieved in 78% (21) of all patients. The authors concluded that based on these findings, the NightLase LAUP treatment of OSA represented a safe and effective therapeutic method. Moreover, these researchers stated that with further prospective, longer-term studies in a multi-disciplinary team to evaluate its effectiveness, this therapy could potentially be integrated into the current guidelines for treating OSA.

These investigators stated that one of the limitations of this trial was that AHI was used as a single endpoint demarcating success; however, a combination of patient-centered (scoring systems) and objective (PSG) outcomes would be preferable. Furthermore, these endpoints should ideally be interpreted together with at least some of the patient's other symptoms and anatomical characteristics (snoring score and reduction, Mallampati classification, Friedman tongue position, respiratory disturbance index, Muller`s maneuver, etc.) and influence on QOL (satisfaction questionnaire, ESS, etc.). Even though AHI was only measured up to 1 month after the last treatment session, even better results could potentially be expected after 2 to 3 months when the process of neocollagenesis would be well established. According to the previous studies, the result of the NightLase treatment will typically last anywhere from 6 to 24 months and is easily touched up at follow-up appointments. Long-term effect of this treatment would need to be determined, but the analysis of charts was done retrospectively and the treatments and/or further objective evaluation of the outcome had been discontinued. It is also important to emphasize that if the obstruction responsible for OSA is not located in the oropharynx but, for example, in the nose or in the level of hyoid bone, the treatment will not be effective because these regions will not be irradiated with this protocol. Careful selection of patients with a multi-disciplinary approach is therefore critical.

In a RCT, Picavet et al (2023) examined the safety and effectiveness of a non-invasive 2,940 nm Er:YAG treatment with SMOOTH mode in reducing snoring in adult patients and compared its safety and effectiveness to sham treatment. A total of 40 primary snoring patients (18 years of age or older, AHI of less than 15 events/hour, BMI of 30 or less) were randomized to receive either 3 sessions NightLase or sham laser treatment. The main outcome measures were Snore Outcomes Survey (SOS), the Spouse/Bed Partner Survey (SBPS), a VAS scale (bed partner) and a VAS (pain). NightLase was well-tolerated, no local anesthesia was required (mean VAS pain score in NightLase group = 3.0 ± 1.7); no complications occurred. SOS, SBPS and VAS snoring scores improved in the NightLase group (33.7 ± 14.1 to 56.2 ± 16.1) (35.0 ± 17.1 to 61.5 ± 16.4) and (7.9 ± 2.0 to 4.7 ± 2.8) while no changing in the sham group (32.2 ± 14.5 versus 32.1 ± 13.0) (36.7 ± 12.1 versus 34.7 ± 12.7) (8.1 ± 1.7 versus 8.0 ± 1.6), respectively. The authors concluded that NightLase was a safe, minimal invasive treatment that significantly reduced snoring compared to sham treatment. Moreover, these researchers stated that further prospective, large-scale and long-term follow-up studies are needed to prove its (long-term) effectiveness. They stated that the findings of this trial are promising; moreover, not all subjects reported an adequate reduction of snoring. The small sample size (n = 20 in each group) and the short follow-up (up to 3 months after last treatment) limited the significance of the conclusions.

The ULTepap System

The ULTepap System is a single-patient, reusable expiratory positive airway pressure (EPAP) device for the treatment of mild-to-moderate OSA marketed as ULTepap, which received the FDA’s 510(k) clearance on January 24, 2020. The device is comprised of a pair of bi-resistance cartridges that are designed and warrantied for a 3-year expected service life. The ULTepap System includes a headgear and appropriate size nasal pillow for the patient. These accessory items are similar in design and performance to currently available products.

AirLift Procedure for Tongue Suspension

The AirLift procedure for tongue suspension using the Encore System entails placement of simple implants in the tongue and lower jaw. The objective of the procedure is to stabilize the tongue in order to prevent obstruction of the upper airway; thus, improving breathing during sleep.

In a retrospective study, Ong et al (2017) examined the effects of hyoid myotomy and suspension (HMS) without concurrent palatal or tongue base sleep surgery for the treatment of OSA. Patients with OSA treated with HMS were identified using CPT code (21685) at an academic and private sleep surgery clinic. Identified patients were limited to those undergoing HMS with the AirLift system. Individuals who underwent concurrent palatal or tongue base sleep surgery were excluded. Outcomes included simultaneous procedures, AHI, LSAT, and ESS. A total of 19 patients with OSA underwent HMS without palatal or tongue base sleep surgery. The average age at surgery was (55.3 ± 13.5) years with a majority of patients being men (71%). Concurrent procedures included the following: torus mandibularis excision (n = 1), endoscopic sinus surgery (n = 4), septoplasty (n = 10), inferior turbinate reduction (n = 12), and nasal valve repair (n = 2). AHI improved significantly from (39.7 ± 21.2) events/hour to (22.6 ± 22.7) events/hour after HMS (p < 0.01), which represented a 43% reduction. LSAT significantly increased from (82.2% ± 9.9%) to (86.6% ± 6.2%), p < 0.01. There was no improvement in ESS after surgery (8.2 ± 4.4) to (8.3 ± 5.2), p = 0.904. A subset of patients with severe OSA (AHI greater than 30 events/hour) had an improvement in AHI from (49.9 ± 16.6) events/hour to (29.1 ± 24.9) events/hour, p < 0.01. The authors concluded that HMS without palatal or tongue base sleep surgery improved OSA severity. It could be considered as a valid option in the treatment of OSA in appropriately-selected patients. Moreover, these researchers stated that future studies should examine patient characteristics and specific anatomic variants which are more likely to successfully respond to this procedure.

The authors stated that drawbacks of this study included its retrospective nature and small sample size (n = 19). Selection bias was important as patients were selected as surgical candidates who were thought to benefit from isolated HMS and did not require additional surgical treatment of the palate or tongue base. Unfortunately, the DISE videos were not available for review to determine whether those who failed required further treatment.

Drug-Induced Sleep Endoscopy (DISE Procedure) for the Treatment of Tracheomalacia

De Lausnay et al (2021) stated that OSA and lower airway anomalies are both highly prevalent in children with Down syndrome (DS); however, little is known regarding the interaction between both. In a retrospective study, these investigators examined the co-occurrence of OSA (defined as obstructive apnea/hypopnea index (oAHI) of 2/hour or higher) and lower airway anomalies in children with DS and examined their impact on OSA severity and treatment outcome. Airway anomalies such as laryngo- and tracheomalacia are also more common in children with DS compared to controls. This trial was a retrospective analysis of data from airway endoscopy and PSG in a cohort of children with DS. Data on both lower airway evaluation and PSG were available for 70 patients with DS. The study population was relatively young (mean age of 3.5 years), not obese, and presented with severe OSA (mean oAHI = 13.1/hour). Airway anomalies were found in 49/70 children (70%), most frequently laryngomalacia, tracheomalacia, or a combined airway malformation. In the remaining 21 cases (30%), endoscopy was normal. A comparison between both groups showed a similar distribution of gender, age and BMI z-scores. The prevalence of OSA was not significantly higher in DS patients with airway anomalies (89.6% versus 71.4%, p = 0.078). Furthermore, OSA severity or treatment choice (conservative, upper airway surgery or CPAP) were not significantly different. Follow-up data (available for 49/70 patients) showed a significant improvement of OSA in both groups. There was not a significant tendency to more patients with persistent OSA among those with lower airway anomalies (34.3% versus 7.1%, p = 0.075). The authors found no significant differences in OSA severity, treatment choice, or outcome between children with DS with and without lower airway anomalies. These researchers stated that further studies should examine the role of DISE-directed treatment and compare the outcome of different therapeutic modalities in larger patient groups.

Elevoplasty / Elevo Palatal Implant System for the Treatment of Snoring

On January 28, 2019, Cook Medical and Zelegent, Inc., announced an FDA clearance for the Elevo Kit Snoring Intervention Device. The specialized tool is designed to enhance therapeutic options for individuals who suffer from snoring. Elevo’s delivery system allows placement of specially-shaped sutures that provide lift to the soft palate and then are naturally dissolved by the body. It is indicated for symptomatic, habitual, and social snoring due to palatal flutter. Elevo is used in elevoplasty, a procedure that provides lift and stiffening to the soft palate tissue; elevoplasty can be carried out under local anesthesia in an office setting without the need for surgery.

However, there is a lack of evidence regarding the effectiveness of elevoplasty/the Elevo Palatal Implant System for the treatment of snoring.

Expiratory Muscle Strength Training for the Treatment of Obstructive Sleep Apnea Syndrome

In a randomized, parallel, double-blinded study, Erturk et al (2024) examined the effects of high and low-intensity expiratory muscle strength training (EMST) on disease severity, systemic inflammation, oxidative stress, respiratory muscle strength, exercise capacity, symptoms, daytime sleepiness, fatigue severity, and sleep quality in male patients with OSAS. A total of 31 male patients diagnosed with moderate OSAS were included in this trial. Subjects were randomized into 2 groups: High-EMST and Low-EMST groups. EMST was used at home 7 days/week, once-daily, for 25 breaths, 12 weeks. Respiratory muscle strength was measured using a mouth pressure device. Disease severity (AHI) and, respiratory sleep events by PSG, total oxidant level (TOS), total antioxidant level (TAS), oxidative stress index (OSI), CRP, tumor necrosis factor-alpha (TNF-α), IL-6), and IL-10 levels by blood (serum) were evaluated. The percentage of AHI change in the High-EMST group (50.8%) was significantly higher than in the Low-EMST group (6.3%) (p = 0.002, d = 1.31). In general, as MEP increased by 1 unit, AHI decreased by 0.149 points (b = -0.149; CR = -3.065; p = 0.002), and as AHI increased by 1 unit, ODI increased by 0.746 points (b = 0.746; CR = 10.604; p < 0.001). TOS, OSI, TNF-α and IL-6 levels decreased at similar rates in both groups. The authors concluded that EMST significantly reduced systemic inflammation and oxidative stress while improving expiratory muscle strength in male patients with moderate OSAS. High-EMST was more effective in enhancing the severity of disease than Low-EMST. These researchers stated that EMST is a practical, effective, and promising treatment for pulmonary rehabilitation in patients with moderate OSAS. This was a relatively small study (n = 31) without a comparative group; its findings need to be validated by well-designed studies.

Gut Microbiome and Obstructive Sleep Apnea

Liu et al (2024) noted that previous studies have identified a clinical association between gut microbiota and OSA; however, the potential causal relationship between the two has not been determined. These researchers employed Mendelian randomization (MR) to examine the potential causal effects of gut microbiota on OSA and the impact of OSA on altering the composition of gut microbiota. Bi-directional MR and replicated validation were used. Summary-level genetic data of gut microbiota were derived from the MiBioGen consortium and the Dutch Microbiome Project (DMP). Summary statistics of OSA were drawn from FinnGen Consortium and Million Veteran Program (MVP). Inverse-variance-weighted (IVW), weighted median, MR-Egger, Simple Mode, and Weighted Mode methods were used to examine the potential causal link between gut microbiota and OSA. These investigators identified potential causal associations between 23 gut microbiota and OSA. Among them, genus Eubacterium xylanophilum group (OR = 0.86; p = 0.00013), Bifidobacterium longum (OR = 0.90; p = 0.0090), Parabacteroides merdae (OR = 0.85; p = 0.00016) retained a strong negative association with OSA following the Bonferroni correction. Reverse MR analyses indicated that OSA was associated with 20 gut microbiota, among them, a strong inverse association between OSA and genus Anaerostipes (beta = -0.35; p = 0.00032) was identified following Bonferroni correction. The authors concluded that the findings of this study implicated the potential bi-directional causal effects of the gut microbiota on OSA, potentially providing new insights into the prevention and treatment of OSA via specific gut microbiota.

The authors stated that this study had several drawbacks. First, in the forward MR analysis, the focus was primarily on populations of European ancestry, which may have limited the generalizability of the results to other populations. In the reverse MR analysis, although the majority of individuals were of European and North American ancestry, the inevitable inclusion of mixed-race individuals may have introduced bias in the results. Second, this MR analysis of the association between gut microbiota and OSA did not explain its mechanisms. Third, these researchers used the summary statistics published and they could not adjust the rules for participation and exclusion; thus, infection and other disease might induce bias to their analysis. Fourth, as the instrumental variables were derived from genome-wide association study (GWAS) meta-analyses, they were unable to examine stratification effects and other non-linear relationships. Moreover, these researchers stated that while observational studies have not yet concluded whether the impact of gut microbiota on OSA risk is linear, the possibility of non-linear models could not be ruled out. In the future, it is anticipated that individual-level GWAS data will be used for non-linear MR studies to further examine the non-linear relationship between gut microbiota and OSA.

Quantitative Susceptibility Mapping

Bai et al (2024) compared whole-brain iron deposition between OSA patients and a healthy control group, we initially utilized QSM and evaluated its correlation with PSG results and cognitive function. A total of 28 OSA patients and 22 healthy controls (HCs) matched in age, education level, and BMI were enrolled in this trial. Each subject underwent scanning with 3D T1 and multi-echo GRE sequences. In addition, PSG results were collected from OSA patients, and they underwent simple cognitive assessments. Lastly, these researchers analyzed the relationship between iron content in different brain regions, PSG results, and cognitive ability. In OSA patients, iron content increased in the left temporal-pole-sup and right putamen, while it decreased in the left fusiform gyrus, left middle temporal gyrus, right inferior occipital gyrus, and right superior temporal gyrus. The correlation analysis between brain iron content and PSG results/cognitive scales was as follows: left fusiform gyrus and MMSE (r = -0.416, p = 0.028); right superior temporal gyrus and MMSE (r = 0.422, p = 0.025); left middle temporal gyrus and average oxygen saturation (r = -0.418, p = 0.027); left temporal-pole-sup and REM stage (rs = 0.466, p = 0.012); the right putamen and N1 stage (rs = 0.393. p = 0.039). Moreover, both MoCA (r = 0.598, p = 0.001) and MMSE (r = 0.456, p = 0.015) revealed a positive correlation with average oxygen saturation. The authors concluded that this study was the first to use QSM technology to show abnormal brain iron levels in OSA. These researchers stated that correlations between brain iron content, PSG, and cognition in OSA may reveal neuropathological mechanisms, aiding OSA diagnosis. 

Genio System

The Genio system is an FDA-approved, mask-free treatment for adults with moderate to severe Obstructive Sleep Apnea (OSA) who cannot tolerate or have failed traditional therapies like CPAP. Developed by Nyxoah, the system works by using hypoglossal nerve stimulation (HGNS) to deliver bilateral (dual-sided) electrical pulses to the tongue muscles during sleep, which moves the tongue forward to keep the airway open. The system consists of a small, battery-free neurostimulator implanted in a single incision under the chin and an external wearable activation chip that powers the implant and is worn nightly via an adhesive patch. Patients can control the discreet, full-body MRI-compatible device using a smartphone app to adjust comfort settings and track progress.

Eastwood et al. (2020) aimed to evaluate the safety and effectiveness of the Genio System, a novel bilateral hypoglossal nerve stimulation (HNS) device for treating moderate-to-severe obstructive sleep apnea (OSA) in adults who were intolerant of positive airway pressure therapy. Conducted as a prospective, open-label, nonrandomized, single-arm trial across eight centers in Australia, France, and the UK, the study implanted 27 participants and followed them for six months. The device consists of a small, battery-free stimulator implanted submentally, activated externally via a patch, delivering bilateral stimulation without respiratory sensing leads. Primary outcomes included the incidence of device-related serious adverse events (SAEs) and changes in apnea–hypopnea index (AHI), while secondary outcomes assessed oxygen desaturation index (ODI), sleep architecture, daytime sleepiness, quality of life, and snoring. Results showed no device-related SAEs, though four procedure-related SAEs occurred, all resolved without sequelae. Mean AHI decreased from 23.7 to 12.9 events/hour (p<0.0001), and ODI dropped from 19.1 to 9.8 events/hour (p<0.0001). Daytime sleepiness and quality-of-life scores improved significantly, and bedpartner-reported loud snoring fell from 96% to 35%. Adherence was high, with 91% of participants using the device more than five nights per week and 77% using it for over five hours per night. Limitations include the small sample size, lack of a control group, short follow-up duration, and reliance on self-reported adherence. Despite these constraints, the authors concluded that this study demonstrated that the Genio system offers a safe, effective, and less invasive alternative to traditional HNS devices, with promising improvements in OSA severity and patient-reported outcomes.

Woodson et al. (2025) aimed to evaluate the safety and efficacy of the Genio bilateral hypoglossal nerve stimulation (HNS BL) device for treating moderate-to-severe obstructive sleep apnea (OSA) in patients intolerant of positive airway pressure therapy. This prospective, multicenter, nonrandomized, single-arm trial enrolled 115 participants who underwent implantation of the Genio system, an externally powered, battery-free device stimulating both hypoglossal nerves. The coprimary endpoints at 12 months were achieving at least a 50% reduction in the apnea-hypopnea index (AHI) with a final AHI <20 events/hour and a 25% reduction in the oxygen desaturation index (ODI). Results showed responder rates of 63.5% for AHI and 71.3% for ODI, with significant improvements in secondary outcomes such as mean AHI, ODI, sleep time with oxygen saturation <90%, and patient-reported measures of sleepiness and quality of life. Snoring severity and daytime symptoms also improved markedly, and most participants reported high satisfaction with therapy. Safety analysis revealed 11 serious adverse events in 10 participants (8.7%), primarily device- or procedure-related, and a high incidence of nonserious events, most resolving within one month. Limitations include the single-arm, open-label design without a control group, a predominantly older, overweight, white male cohort limiting generalizability, reliance on self-reported adherence, and attrition of 23.5% of participants. Despite these constraints, the authors concluded that this study demonstrated clinically meaningful improvements and an acceptable safety profile, suggesting HNS BL as a promising alternative for select OSA patients.

Glossary of Terms

Table: Glossary of Terms
Term Definition
Apnea Temporary cessation of breathing, especially during sleep
Apnea-hypopnea index (AHI) Scale that measures sleep apnea severity, which includes the average number of episodes of apnea and hypopnea per hour
Automatic positive airway pressure (APAP) Ventilation device that delivers positive air pressure which automatically self-adjusts based on a person’s breathing and need to keep airway open
Bilevel positive airway pressure (BiPAP) Ventilation device that delivers different positive air pressures upon inhaling (higher pressure) and exhaling (lower pressure) to keep airway open
Continuous positive airway pressure (CPAP) Ventilation device that continuously delivers the same amount of positive air pressure during inspiration (inhaling) and expiration (exhalation) to keep airway open
Hypopnea Partial reduction of airflow in the airway resulting in abnormally slow or shallow breathing
Obstructive sleep apnea (OSA) Sleep-related breathing disorder that involves a decrease or complete halt in airflow despite an ongoing effort to breathe. It occurs when the muscles relax during sleep, causing soft tissue in the back of the throat to collapse and block the upper airway. This leads to hypopneas and apneas in breathing.
Positive airway pressure (PAP) Uses a machine to pump air under pressure into the airway of the lungs
Polysomnography (PSG) Sleep study; a comprehensive test used to diagnose sleep disorders
Positional therapy Strategy for treating snoring and sleep apnea which involves wearing a device around the chest or waist to help prevent a person from laying in a supine position (on their back)
Respiratory disturbance index (RDI) Combined number of apneas, hypopneas, and RERAs per hour of sleep
Respiratory effort related arousal (RERA) Event that causes an arousal or a decrease in oxygen saturation, without qualifying as an apnea or hypopnea
Uvulopalatopharyngoplasty (UPPP) Surgery to open the upper airways by taking out extra tissue in the throat
Upper airway stimulation (UAS) therapy Involves implanting a small device that senses breathing patterns and delivers mild stimulation to a nerve in the throat with each breath to keep tissue in the throat and tongue from blocking the airway

Indications for Obstructive Sleep Apnea Testing

Testing for OSA is considered medically necessary for individuals who present with clinical features suggestive of moderate to severe OSA as evidenced by:

  • Excessive daytime sleepiness (EDS) and one of the following are present:

    • BMI greater than 30; or
    • Excessive sleepiness while driving; or
    • Loud/intense snoring; or
  • Epworth Sleepiness Scale (ESS) score of 10 or greater; or
  • Witnessed nocturnal apnea, choking and/or gasping.

Note: The International Classification of Sleep Disorders, third edition (ICSD-3) defines EDS as the inability to maintain wakefulness and alertness during the major waking episodes of the day, with sleep occurring unintentionally or at inappropriate times almost daily for at least three months (AASM, 2014).

Epworth Sleepiness Scale

Indicate the likelihood of falling asleep in the following commonly encountered situations. Assign the following scores to the patient's responses:

Table 1: Epworth Sleepiness Scale
Likelihood of dozing Score
None 0
Low Chance 1
Moderate Chance 2
High Chance 3
  1. Sitting and reading
  2. Watching TV
  3. Sitting, inactive, in a public place, i.e., theater
  4. As a passenger in a car for an hour without a break
  5. Lying down to rest in the afternoon when circumstances permit
  6. Sitting and talking to someone
  7. In a car, while stopped for a few minutes in traffic.

Sum the scores. A total greater than 10 is considered abnormal.

Monitoring Devices

Table 2: Monitoring Devices
Type Devices
I Comprehensive standard overnight polysomnography in a sleep center or laboratory with a sleep technician in constant attendance. Minimum of 7 parameters including EEG, EOG, chin EMG, ECG or heart rate, airflow, respiratory effort, oxygen saturation
II Comprehensive, portable sleep study Minimum of 7 parameters including EEG, EOG, chin EMG, ECG or heart rate, airflow, respiratory effort, oxygen saturation
III Modified portable sleep apnea testing Minimum of 4 parameters, including ventilation (at least 2 channels of respiratory movement, or respiratory movement and airflow), heart rate or ECG, oxygen saturation)
IV(A) Three or more bio-parameters Airflow and at least 2 other parameters (e.g., EOG, peripheral arterial tonometry (PAT), snoring, actigraphy, pulse oximetry)
IV(B) Continuous single- or dual-bio-parameter recording Minimum of 1 parameter (e.g., overnight oximetry) and does not meet criteria for Types I to III or Type IV(A) device.

Usual Medically Necessary Quantities of Positive Airway Pressure Supplies

Table 3: Usual Medically Necessary Quantities of Positive Airway Pressure Supplies
Supply Description Quantity
Tubing with integrated heating element for use with positive airway pressure device 1 per 3 months
Combination oral/nasal mask, used with continuous positive airway pressure, each 1 per 3 months
Oral cushion for combination oral/nasal mask, replacement only 2 per 1 month
Nasal pillows for combination oral/nasal mask 2 per 1 month
Full face mask used with positive airway pressure device 1 per 3 months
Full face mask interface, replacement for full face mask 1 per 1 month
Cushion for use on nasal mask interface 2 per 1 month
Pillow for use on nasal cannula type interface 2 per 1 month
Nasal interface (mask or cannula type, used with positive airway pressure 1 per 3 months
Headgear used with positive airway pressure device 1 per 6 months
Chinstrap used with positive airway pressure device 1 per 6 months
Tubing used with positive airway pressure device 1 per 3 months
Filter, disposable, used with positive airway pressure device 2 per 1 month
Filter, non-disposable, used with positive airway pressure device 1 per 6 months
Water chamber for humidifier, used with positive airway pressure 1 per 6 months
